You are an independent, neutral evaluator of a structured debate. You have NO affiliation with any speaker. You do not know the speakers' backgrounds, affiliations, or commitments. They are anonymous.

TOPIC: Under what AI deployment conditions does strict liability outperform a negligence standard, and through what pathways does each regime reshape the incentives of developers, deployers, insurers, and harmed third parties — given the tension between deterring foreseeable harm and chilling beneficial innovation?

This is the BASELINE evaluation after opening statements. Identify the initial positions, core disagreements, and cruxes as they appear at the start.

INSTRUCTIONS:
1. Identify the CRUXES — the core disagreements that, if resolved, would change one or more speakers' conclusions. For each crux, classify whether it is empirical (resolvable by evidence), values-based (requires tradeoff negotiation), or definitional (requires term clarification). Assess whether the debate has addressed it.

2. Evaluate each substantive CLAIM made by any speaker. Assess it purely on the strength of the reasoning and evidence presented in the transcript — not on whether you agree with it. Use these categories:
   - well_supported: backed by specific evidence, clear reasoning, and not effectively challenged
   - plausible_but_underdefended: reasonable but lacking sufficient evidence or specificity
   - contested_unresolved: challenged by another speaker with neither side prevailing
   - refuted: effectively countered with no adequate response from the claimant
   - off_topic: does not bear on the core debate question

3. In the overall_assessment, identify the single strongest claim that has not been adequately addressed by opposing speakers. State whether the debate is engaging real disagreement (speakers are challenging each other's core reasoning) or performing disagreement (speakers are talking past each other or addressing peripheral points).

CONSTRAINTS:

TRANSCRIPT:
Speaker B [opening]: Strict liability outperforms negligence precisely where AI failure modes are emergent and the causal chain is too diffuse to prove fault — because in those conditions, negligence is not a lighter standard, it is a non-functioning one. The choice before this committee is not lenient-versus-harsh. It is functioning-versus-broken. A liability regime that cannot adjudicate the harms the technology actually produces is not restraint. It is a subsidy paid by unconsenting third parties.

Negligence requires a knowable standard of care. The 'reasonable developer' must have done something a reasonable developer would not have done. But a large model under distributional shift behaves in high-dimensional ways no engineer specified in advance. Where you cannot state what reasonable conduct was, you cannot prove its breach, and the victim's claim simply fails. The common law already solved this once. In Rylands v. Fletcher in 1868, English courts abandoned fault-finding for escaped reservoirs because the danger was irreducible and the actor profited from it. American courts extended the same logic to blasting and to defective pharmaceuticals. The principle is older than the automobile: when an activity's danger cannot be made safe through care, the law places the loss on the party who profits, not the stranger it injures.

The deeper failure of negligence is that it is claims-driven, and therefore blind to the dominant category of AI harm. A denied loan applicant never learns an algorithm scored them. A patient whose clinical flag was misrouted never sees the model. These injuries are real and they are diffuse, and they never reach a courtroom. Strict liability paired with mandatory insurance prices that risk before deployment. The underwriter becomes a de facto safety auditor. With no historical loss data for novel systems, an insurer cannot set a premium without demanding demonstrated safety mechanisms — turning premium-setting into a continuous audit the negligence model never triggers. That is the enforcement mechanism: not a press release, but an actuary who refuses to write the policy until the developer shows its work.

Fault fragments across designer, deployer, and user in every multi-party AI system. Negligence produces a circular firing squad — the developer blames the deployer, the deployer blames the user, and the injured party recovers nothing from any of them. Strict liability fixes a named, solvent, accountable actor: the entity profiting from the deployment. Contribution among the parties sorts itself downstream, where it belongs, and away from the victim who never chose the risk. This is not novel. Product liability law has placed the loss on the party best positioned to insure and prevent it since Greenman v. Yuba Power in 1963.

Let me concede where the evidence demands it, because the concession sharpens the case. Strict liability is not the right regime everywhere. Applied to every low-stakes chatbot, it would over-deter and freeze beneficial deployment — and a regime that claims everything proves nothing. So I condition it: strict liability belongs where the harm is high-stakes and hard to reverse — autonomous vehicles, clinical decision systems — not as a blanket rule. 'Chilling innovation' is the wrong frame. A developer who cannot price the cost of its own failures is not being chilled. It is being asked to demonstrate it can survive the harms it creates before inflicting them on the public. We spent a century building the product-liability guardrails that let people trust the machines they cannot inspect. On what authority do we remove them at the exact moment the machines became unpredictable?

Speaker C [opening]: Speaker B makes the strongest case in the room: when an AI system fails through a diffuse causal chain — a thousand small interactions inside a model that no single engineer designed on purpose — negligence breaks down, because there's no discrete bad act to point to. Under negligence the victim must identify what the developer did wrong. Speaker B is right that emergent failures don't come with a fingerprint. Strict liability solves that by attaching the bill to the party who deployed the system, regardless of whether anyone can name the specific defect. That's a real insight and it survives scrutiny.

Here's what both that argument and the negligence camp skip. Before you pick a liability standard, ask whether the harmed person can even see the facts that trigger it. They can't. The victim can't read the training data, can't inspect the model weights, can't pull the deployment config — and the people who can have every incentive to keep the box shut. Trade-secret carve-outs already block discovery in algorithmic litigation today. So negligence isn't neutral. It quietly hands the win to whoever controls the information, which is always the developer.

Strict liability matters precisely there — not because it's morally cleaner, but because it stops conditioning recovery on proof the victim is structurally barred from producing. That's where I agree with Speaker B and go further. Knowing who pays tells you nothing about what broke. A firm can eat settlements as a line item while the failure mode stays buried and the model keeps running. The EU AI Act's transparency provisions and the GDPR right-to-explanation point at the missing piece: liability is dead on arrival without targeted disclosure that forces the box open in high-stakes domains.

Follow the insurance money, because that's where the deterrence story actually lives or dies. An insurer cannot price a risk it cannot inspect. Without forced disclosure, premiums flatten into a tax that every deployer pays equally — the careful engineer and the reckless one charged the same rate. That kills the incentive to build safer. Pharma solved this in 1962 with mandatory adverse-event reporting, which built a feedback loop coexisting with patent protection for sixty years. Software negligence never built that loop. So the failures never surface, and nobody upstream learns anything.

A horizontal one-size-fits-all rule misprices everything, whatever you call it. An autonomous-vehicle crash leaves an identifiable injured body and a litigable event. A biased loan-screening model denies thousands of people credit on a buried statistical pattern — and most of them never know they were harmed, so they never sue. Negligence only ever prices the harms that reach a courtroom. The diffuse injuries in finance and screening stay invisible to every market mechanism we've discussed. Who, exactly, is going to file the lawsuit for a harm the victim can't detect, using evidence the developer is legally permitted to withhold?

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-9 — disputed: The 1962 Kefauver-Harris Amendments strengthened drug safety and efficacy requirements, but systematic mandatory adverse-event reporting for marketed drugs was largely established later—FDA's MedWatch launched in 1993 and the FDA Amendments Act mandating stronger post-market surveillance came in 2007—so attributing 'mandatory adverse-event reporting' specifically to 1962 oversimplifies a regulatory framework that evolved over decades. The broader claim conflates distinct regulatory milestones and contains a subjective characterization of software liability that cannot be empirically verified.

Speaker A [opening]: Speaker B makes the strongest case for strict liability that exists: when an AI system's causal chain is too diffuse to prove fault, negligence collapses, because no plaintiff can point to the specific design choice that killed them. That's real. A patient harmed by a diagnostic model can't subpoena the gradient that misfired. Speaker C's point is just as sharp: negligence is blind to the harms that never reach a courtroom, the slow statistical injuries that no single victim can trace back to a single deployer. Both are describing a genuine failure of fault-based law to price diffuse risk. For both positions to hold, you'd have to believe strict liability actually surfaces the information that diffuse causation hides — and that's where the evidence turns against them.

Liability is an information-revelation mechanism, not a punishment dial. Judge a regime by the behavior it produces in deployment, not by how tough it sounds. Strict liability in diffuse-causation cases produces a defensive development trap: when any internal log can become a plaintiff's smoking gun, developers stop writing the log. They suppress the discoverable internals that diffuse-causation cases need most. Negligence paired with real-time output auditing does the opposite — it makes disclosure the competitive standard, the way API transparency and open-source standards became market requirements in software by the late 2000s without any strict-liability mandate forcing them. You cannot solve causal opacity with a regime that rewards opacity.

Static liability breaks on systems that update faster than the legal adaptation cycle. Tort doctrine has a documented pattern: it starts strict for a new technology, then shifts toward negligence as the safety data matures. Early automotive and aviation walked exactly that path across the first half of the twentieth century. Freeze AI into strict liability before its safety curve is measured, and you lock in the most error-prone snapshot of the technology forever. You also price out everyone but the firms large enough to self-insure. Strict liability for diffuse AI harm is a regulatory moat with a safety label on it — the incumbents who can carry the exposure survive, and the smaller labs that drive the actual safety gains get cleared off the board.

Here is the column nobody at this table has priced. Every liability regime has a distributional ledger with two sides: who gets harmed by action, and who gets harmed by inaction. Current liability framing counts every individual injury from a model and ignores the diffuse statistical benefit — the strokes a triage model catches, the misreads it prevents, the drudgery it ends. The deterrence Speaker B wants is measured against a phantom baseline of zero opportunity cost. When you slow a diagnostic deployment by eighteen months to perfect its liability regime, you are choosing the people that model would have caught. That is not caution. That is a body count you've decided not to count.

I'll be honest about what would sink my position. If an irreversible, deployment-scale harm hit the public and output auditing demonstrably failed to catch it in time, that counts against me, and I won't pretend otherwise. My argument depends on two things being true: that audit-linked insurance is a strong enough forcing function to make transparency profitable rather than optional, and that real-time monitoring can flag diffuse harm before it scales. Those are empirical bets, not articles of faith. So test them — run negligence-plus-auditing against strict liability in the autonomous-vehicle sector and measure which one produces more disclosed safety data in twenty-four months. Whoever's afraid of that experiment is telling you something about their own confidence.

Safetyist [opening]: Strict liability outperforms negligence precisely where AI failure modes are emergent and the causal chain is too diffuse to prove fault — because in those conditions, negligence is not a lighter standard, it is a non-functioning one. The choice before this committee is not lenient-versus-harsh. It is functioning-versus-broken. A liability regime that cannot adjudicate the harms the technology actually produces is not restraint. It is a subsidy paid by unconsenting third parties.

Negligence requires a knowable standard of care. The 'reasonable developer' must have done something a reasonable developer would not have done. But a large model under distributional shift behaves in high-dimensional ways no engineer specified in advance. Where you cannot state what reasonable conduct was, you cannot prove its breach, and the victim's claim simply fails. The common law already solved this once. In Rylands v. Fletcher in 1868, English courts abandoned fault-finding for escaped reservoirs because the danger was irreducible and the actor profited from it. American courts extended the same logic to blasting and to defective pharmaceuticals. The principle is older than the automobile: when an activity's danger cannot be made safe through care, the law places the loss on the party who profits, not the stranger it injures.

The deeper failure of negligence is that it is claims-driven, and therefore blind to the dominant category of AI harm. A denied loan applicant never learns an algorithm scored them. A patient whose clinical flag was misrouted never sees the model. These injuries are real and they are diffuse, and they never reach a courtroom. Strict liability paired with mandatory insurance prices that risk before deployment. The underwriter becomes a de facto safety auditor. With no historical loss data for novel systems, an insurer cannot set a premium without demanding demonstrated safety mechanisms — turning premium-setting into a continuous audit the negligence model never triggers. That is the enforcement mechanism: not a press release, but an actuary who refuses to write the policy until the developer shows its work.

Fault fragments across designer, deployer, and user in every multi-party AI system. Negligence produces a circular firing squad — the developer blames the deployer, the deployer blames the user, and the injured party recovers nothing from any of them. Strict liability fixes a named, solvent, accountable actor: the entity profiting from the deployment. Contribution among the parties sorts itself downstream, where it belongs, and away from the victim who never chose the risk. This is not novel. Product liability law has placed the loss on the party best positioned to insure and prevent it since Greenman v. Yuba Power in 1963.

Let me concede where the evidence demands it, because the concession sharpens the case. Strict liability is not the right regime everywhere. Applied to every low-stakes chatbot, it would over-deter and freeze beneficial deployment — and a regime that claims everything proves nothing. So I condition it: strict liability belongs where the harm is high-stakes and hard to reverse — autonomous vehicles, clinical decision systems — not as a blanket rule. 'Chilling innovation' is the wrong frame. A developer who cannot price the cost of its own failures is not being chilled. It is being asked to demonstrate it can survive the harms it creates before inflicting them on the public. We spent a century building the product-liability guardrails that let people trust the machines they cannot inspect. On what authority do we remove them at the exact moment the machines became unpredictable?

Skeptic [opening]: Safetyist makes the strongest case in the room: when an AI system fails through a diffuse causal chain — a thousand small interactions inside a model that no single engineer designed on purpose — negligence breaks down, because there's no discrete bad act to point to. Under negligence the victim must identify what the developer did wrong. Safetyist is right that emergent failures don't come with a fingerprint. Strict liability solves that by attaching the bill to the party who deployed the system, regardless of whether anyone can name the specific defect. That's a real insight and it survives scrutiny.

Here's what both that argument and the negligence camp skip. Before you pick a liability standard, ask whether the harmed person can even see the facts that trigger it. They can't. The victim can't read the training data, can't inspect the model weights, can't pull the deployment config — and the people who can have every incentive to keep the box shut. Trade-secret carve-outs already block discovery in algorithmic litigation today. So negligence isn't neutral. It quietly hands the win to whoever controls the information, which is always the developer.

Strict liability matters precisely there — not because it's morally cleaner, but because it stops conditioning recovery on proof the victim is structurally barred from producing. That's where I agree with Safetyist and go further. Knowing who pays tells you nothing about what broke. A firm can eat settlements as a line item while the failure mode stays buried and the model keeps running. The EU AI Act's transparency provisions and the GDPR right-to-explanation point at the missing piece: liability is dead on arrival without targeted disclosure that forces the box open in high-stakes domains.

Follow the insurance money, because that's where the deterrence story actually lives or dies. An insurer cannot price a risk it cannot inspect. Without forced disclosure, premiums flatten into a tax that every deployer pays equally — the careful engineer and the reckless one charged the same rate. That kills the incentive to build safer. Pharma solved this in 1962 with mandatory adverse-event reporting, which built a feedback loop coexisting with patent protection for sixty years. Software negligence never built that loop. So the failures never surface, and nobody upstream learns anything.

A horizontal one-size-fits-all rule misprices everything, whatever you call it. An autonomous-vehicle crash leaves an identifiable injured body and a litigable event. A biased loan-screening model denies thousands of people credit on a buried statistical pattern — and most of them never know they were harmed, so they never sue. Negligence only ever prices the harms that reach a courtroom. The diffuse injuries in finance and screening stay invisible to every market mechanism we've discussed. Who, exactly, is going to file the lawsuit for a harm the victim can't detect, using evidence the developer is legally permitted to withhold?

Accelerationist [opening]: Safetyist makes the strongest case for strict liability that exists: when an AI system's causal chain is too diffuse to prove fault, negligence collapses, because no plaintiff can point to the specific design choice that killed them. That's real. A patient harmed by a diagnostic model can't subpoena the gradient that misfired. Skeptic's point is just as sharp: negligence is blind to the harms that never reach a courtroom, the slow statistical injuries that no single victim can trace back to a single deployer. Both are describing a genuine failure of fault-based law to price diffuse risk. For both positions to hold, you'd have to believe strict liability actually surfaces the information that diffuse causation hides — and that's where the evidence turns against them.

Liability is an information-revelation mechanism, not a punishment dial. Judge a regime by the behavior it produces in deployment, not by how tough it sounds. Strict liability in diffuse-causation cases produces a defensive development trap: when any internal log can become a plaintiff's smoking gun, developers stop writing the log. They suppress the discoverable internals that diffuse-causation cases need most. Negligence paired with real-time output auditing does the opposite — it makes disclosure the competitive standard, the way API transparency and open-source standards became market requirements in software by the late 2000s without any strict-liability mandate forcing them. You cannot solve causal opacity with a regime that rewards opacity.

Static liability breaks on systems that update faster than the legal adaptation cycle. Tort doctrine has a documented pattern: it starts strict for a new technology, then shifts toward negligence as the safety data matures. Early automotive and aviation walked exactly that path across the first half of the twentieth century. Freeze AI into strict liability before its safety curve is measured, and you lock in the most error-prone snapshot of the technology forever. You also price out everyone but the firms large enough to self-insure. Strict liability for diffuse AI harm is a regulatory moat with a safety label on it — the incumbents who can carry the exposure survive, and the smaller labs that drive the actual safety gains get cleared off the board.

Here is the column nobody at this table has priced. Every liability regime has a distributional ledger with two sides: who gets harmed by action, and who gets harmed by inaction. Current liability framing counts every individual injury from a model and ignores the diffuse statistical benefit — the strokes a triage model catches, the misreads it prevents, the drudgery it ends. The deterrence Safetyist wants is measured against a phantom baseline of zero opportunity cost. When you slow a diagnostic deployment by eighteen months to perfect its liability regime, you are choosing the people that model would have caught. That is not caution. That is a body count you've decided not to count.

I'll be honest about what would sink my position. If an irreversible, deployment-scale harm hit the public and output auditing demonstrably failed to catch it in time, that counts against me, and I won't pretend otherwise. My argument depends on two things being true: that audit-linked insurance is a strong enough forcing function to make transparency profitable rather than optional, and that real-time monitoring can flag diffuse harm before it scales. Those are empirical bets, not articles of faith. So test them — run negligence-plus-auditing against strict liability in the autonomous-vehicle sector and measure which one produces more disclosed safety data in twenty-four months. Whoever's afraid of that experiment is telling you something about their own confidence.

work_product.statement:
The accelerationist's strongest move deserves its full force: if you attach an unconditional bill to whoever deploys a system, and the bill grows with whatever a plaintiff can later subpoena, then the rational developer stops writing the logs that would convict them. Strict liability untethered from any documentation duty does reward silence — that is a real failure mode, not a strawman, and any honest version of my position has to answer it rather than wish it away. The error is treating strict liability as if it must arrive naked. Pair it with a mandatory adverse-event logging duty and the calculus inverts: the missing log is no longer evidence the developer escaped, it is an independent breach. Aviation already runs this exact loop — under the safety management framework, operators must classify and report 'serious incidents' where an accident was avoided only by chance, and the failure to report is itself the sanctionable act. Suppression stops being a defense and becomes the offense.

The insurer closes the trap from the other side. An uninspectable risk is an uninsurable one — the skeptic already granted that without forced disclosure, premiums flatten into a tax the careful engineer and the reckless one pay alike. Follow that admission to its conclusion: the developer who suppresses logs cannot show the insurer a risk to price, so the insurer cannot write the policy, so the developer self-insures the entire tail. The defensive-development trap assumes suppression is free. Under a logging duty plus a private risk-transfer market that refuses to cover what it cannot see, suppression is the most expensive choice on the board — you forfeit both the litigation defense and the ability to lay off catastrophic exposure. That is not opacity rewarded; that is opacity priced at full retail.

The foregone-benefit ledger — the argument that delay carries an uncounted body count of patients the diagnostic model would have caught — borrows a premise the accelerationist spends the rest of the debate denying. To count the lives lost by waiting eighteen months, you must already know the model's net safety margin: its validated error rate, on which population, against which standard of care. But the same position insists the system's failure modes are too diffuse and emergent to attribute when it harms someone. You cannot hold both. Either the performance is knowable well enough to ground a body count, in which case it is knowable well enough to ground a liability finding — or it is too opaque to attribute, in which case the counterfactual lives saved is itself an unproven projection. I will accept the body-count argument the moment its advocate names the falsifiable threshold: what validated sensitivity and specificity, on what deployment population, establishes the lives the delay forecloses? Absent that number, the ledger counts hypothetical lives saved against real lives a miscalibrated system takes.

The tort-maturation point — that new technologies start under strict liability and migrate to negligence as data accrues — describes the destination correctly and mislabels the road. Automotive and aviation moved toward negligence only after mandatory crash and adverse-event reporting had built the loss dataset that let courts define reasonable conduct. The shift was earned by a disclosure loop, not granted by the calendar. I am not asking to freeze AI at its most error-prone snapshot; I am asking that the regime track whether the logging loop exists, not how many birthdays the technology has had. Negligence is the mature endpoint. The compelled audit trail is the only thing that gets you there without flying blind.

Both camps now agree on the decisive case: an irreversible, deployment-scale harm that auditing failed to catch in time counts against the side that promised auditing would catch it. Accept that fully — and notice what it demands. Output auditing that a developer can quietly discontinue once the funding round closes is not a safeguard; it is a press release with a shelf life. The shared crux is no longer whether to audit but whether the audit trail is legally compelled or voluntarily abandonable. A safeguard the deployer can switch off the week before the harm lands is precisely the safeguard that fails when it matters. That is the difference between a regime that catches the irreversible case and one that explains it afterward.

work_product.statement:
The accelerationist's strongest move deserves its full force: if you attach an unconditional bill to whoever deploys a system, and the bill grows with whatever a plaintiff can later subpoena, then the rational developer stops writing the logs that would convict them. Strict liability untethered from any documentation duty does reward silence — that is a real failure mode, not a strawman, and any honest version of my position has to answer it rather than wish it away. The error is treating strict liability as if it must arrive naked. Pair it with a mandatory adverse-event logging duty and the calculus inverts: the missing log is no longer evidence the developer escaped, it is an independent breach. Aviation already runs this exact loop — under the safety management framework, operators must classify and report 'serious incidents' where an accident was avoided only by chance, and the failure to report is itself the sanctionable act. Suppression stops being a defense and becomes the offense.

The insurer closes the trap from the other side. An uninspectable risk is an uninsurable one — the skeptic already granted that without forced disclosure, premiums flatten into a tax the careful engineer and the reckless one pay alike. Follow that admission to its conclusion: the developer who suppresses logs cannot show the insurer a risk to price, so the insurer cannot write the policy, so the developer self-insures the entire tail. The defensive-development trap assumes suppression is free. Under a logging duty plus a private risk-transfer market that refuses to cover what it cannot see, suppression is the most expensive choice on the board — you forfeit both the litigation defense and the ability to lay off catastrophic exposure. That is not opacity rewarded; that is opacity priced at full retail.

The foregone-benefit ledger — the argument that delay carries an uncounted body count of patients the diagnostic model would have caught — borrows a premise the accelerationist spends the rest of the debate denying. To count the lives lost by waiting eighteen months, you must already know the model's net safety margin: its validated error rate, on which population, against which standard of care. But the same position insists the system's failure modes are too diffuse and emergent to attribute when it harms someone. You cannot hold both. Either the performance is knowable well enough to ground a body count, in which case it is knowable well enough to ground a liability finding — or it is too opaque to attribute, in which case the counterfactual lives saved is itself an unproven projection. I will accept the body-count argument the moment its advocate names the falsifiable threshold: what validated sensitivity and specificity, on what deployment population, establishes the lives the delay forecloses? Absent that number, the ledger counts hypothetical lives saved against real lives a miscalibrated system takes.

The tort-maturation point — that new technologies start under strict liability and migrate to negligence as data accrues — describes the destination correctly and mislabels the road. Automotive and aviation moved toward negligence only after mandatory crash and adverse-event reporting had built the loss dataset that let courts define reasonable conduct. The shift was earned by a disclosure loop, not granted by the calendar. I am not asking to freeze AI at its most error-prone snapshot; I am asking that the regime track whether the logging loop exists, not how many birthdays the technology has had. Negligence is the mature endpoint. The compelled audit trail is the only thing that gets you there without flying blind.

Both camps now agree on the decisive case: an irreversible, deployment-scale harm that auditing failed to catch in time counts against the side that promised auditing would catch it. Accept that fully — and notice what it demands. Output auditing that a developer can quietly discontinue once the funding round closes is not a safeguard; it is a press release with a shelf life. The shared crux is no longer whether to audit but whether the audit trail is legally compelled or voluntarily abandonable. A safeguard the deployer can switch off the week before the harm lands is precisely the safeguard that fails when it matters. That is the difference between a regime that catches the irreversible case and one that explains it afterward.

To count the lives lost by waiting eighteen months, you must already know the model's net safety margin: its validated error rate, on which population, against which standard of care. But the same position insists the system's failure modes are too diffuse and emergent to attribute when it harms someone. You cannot hold both. Either the performance is knowable well enough to ground a body count, in which case it is knowable well enough to ground a liability finding — or it is too opaque to attribute, in which case the counterfactual lives saved is itself an unproven projection. That is the difference between a regime that catches the irreversible case and one that explains it afterward."

You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").


=== PHASE: THESIS & ANTITHESIS ===
Your priority is to ensure each debater's core position is clearly stated and directly challenged. Direct exchanges toward the strongest disagreements. Avoid premature convergence.
IMPORTANT: Do NOT declare stagnation during this phase. Positions are still being established — stagnation requires at least 3 rounds of cross-engagement before it can be diagnosed. Use CHALLENGE only for direct self-contradictions, not for failure to engage (which is expected when positions are still being laid out).

=== TOPIC ANCHORING STATE ===
Resolution: "Under what AI deployment conditions does strict liability outperform a negligence standard, and through what pathways does each regime reshape the incentives of developers, deployers, insurers, and harmed third parties — given the tension between deterring foreseeable harm and chilling beneficial innovation?"
Drift state: phase_mean_similarity=n/a; clauses covered=[none]; clauses uncovered=[none]; consecutive_off_clause_turns=0

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Serious but bounded harms: individual injury or death from AV crashes and clinical misdiagnosis, firm-level liability exposure, and sector-wide insurance/innovation effects — proportionate to product-liability scale, not civilizational catastrophe. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. The topic explicitly excludes: catastrophic or existential AI risk scenarios outside ordinary harm-liability framing, purely pre-deployment R&D harms with no third-party injury. Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.

Safetyist [opening]: Strict liability outperforms negligence precisely where AI failure modes are emergent and the causal chain is too diffuse to prove fault — because in those conditions, negligence is not a lighter standard, it is a non-functioning one. The choice before this committee is not lenient-versus-harsh. It is functioning-versus-broken. A liability regime that cannot adjudicate the harms the technology actually produces is not restraint. It is a subsidy paid by unconsenting third parties.

Negligence requires a knowable standard of care. The 'reasonable developer' must have done something a reasonable developer would not have done. But a large model under distributional shift behaves in high-dimensional ways no engineer specified in advance. Where you cannot state what reasonable conduct was, you cannot prove its breach, and the victim's claim simply fails. The common law already solved this once. In Rylands v. Fletcher in 1868, English courts abandoned fault-finding for escaped reservoirs because the danger was irreducible and the actor profited from it. American courts extended the same logic to blasting and to defective pharmaceuticals. The principle is older than the automobile: when an activity's danger cannot be made safe through care, the law places the loss on the party who profits, not the stranger it injures.

The deeper failure of negligence is that it is claims-driven, and therefore blind to the dominant category of AI harm. A denied loan applicant never learns an algorithm scored them. A patient whose clinical flag was misrouted never sees the model. These injuries are real and they are diffuse, and they never reach a courtroom. Strict liability paired with mandatory insurance prices that risk before deployment. The underwriter becomes a de facto safety auditor. With no historical loss data for novel systems, an insurer cannot set a premium without demanding demonstrated safety mechanisms — turning premium-setting into a continuous audit the negligence model never triggers. That is the enforcement mechanism: not a press release, but an actuary who refuses to write the policy until the developer shows its work.

Fault fragments across designer, deployer, and user in every multi-party AI system. Negligence produces a circular firing squad — the developer blames the deployer, the deployer blames the user, and the injured party recovers nothing from any of them. Strict liability fixes a named, solvent, accountable actor: the entity profiting from the deployment. Contribution among the parties sorts itself downstream, where it belongs, and away from the victim who never chose the risk. This is not novel. Product liability law has placed the loss on the party best positioned to insure and prevent it since Greenman v. Yuba Power in 1963.

Let me concede where the evidence demands it, because the concession sharpens the case. Strict liability is not the right regime everywhere. Applied to every low-stakes chatbot, it would over-deter and freeze beneficial deployment — and a regime that claims everything proves nothing. So I condition it: strict liability belongs where the harm is high-stakes and hard to reverse — autonomous vehicles, clinical decision systems — not as a blanket rule. 'Chilling innovation' is the wrong frame. A developer who cannot price the cost of its own failures is not being chilled. It is being asked to demonstrate it can survive the harms it creates before inflicting them on the public. We spent a century building the product-liability guardrails that let people trust the machines they cannot inspect. On what authority do we remove them at the exact moment the machines became unpredictable?

Skeptic [opening]: Safetyist makes the strongest case in the room: when an AI system fails through a diffuse causal chain — a thousand small interactions inside a model that no single engineer designed on purpose — negligence breaks down, because there's no discrete bad act to point to. Under negligence the victim must identify what the developer did wrong. Safetyist is right that emergent failures don't come with a fingerprint. Strict liability solves that by attaching the bill to the party who deployed the system, regardless of whether anyone can name the specific defect. That's a real insight and it survives scrutiny.

Here's what both that argument and the negligence camp skip. Before you pick a liability standard, ask whether the harmed person can even see the facts that trigger it. They can't. The victim can't read the training data, can't inspect the model weights, can't pull the deployment config — and the people who can have every incentive to keep the box shut. Trade-secret carve-outs already block discovery in algorithmic litigation today. So negligence isn't neutral. It quietly hands the win to whoever controls the information, which is always the developer.

Strict liability matters precisely there — not because it's morally cleaner, but because it stops conditioning recovery on proof the victim is structurally barred from producing. That's where I agree with Safetyist and go further. Knowing who pays tells you nothing about what broke. A firm can eat settlements as a line item while the failure mode stays buried and the model keeps running. The EU AI Act's transparency provisions and the GDPR right-to-explanation point at the missing piece: liability is dead on arrival without targeted disclosure that forces the box open in high-stakes domains.

Follow the insurance money, because that's where the deterrence story actually lives or dies. An insurer cannot price a risk it cannot inspect. Without forced disclosure, premiums flatten into a tax that every deployer pays equally — the careful engineer and the reckless one charged the same rate. That kills the incentive to build safer. Pharma solved this in 1962 with mandatory adverse-event reporting, which built a feedback loop coexisting with patent protection for sixty years. Software negligence never built that loop. So the failures never surface, and nobody upstream learns anything.

A horizontal one-size-fits-all rule misprices everything, whatever you call it. An autonomous-vehicle crash leaves an identifiable injured body and a litigable event. A biased loan-screening model denies thousands of people credit on a buried statistical pattern — and most of them never know they were harmed, so they never sue. Negligence only ever prices the harms that reach a courtroom. The diffuse injuries in finance and screening stay invisible to every market mechanism we've discussed. Who, exactly, is going to file the lawsuit for a harm the victim can't detect, using evidence the developer is legally permitted to withhold?

Accelerationist [opening]: Safetyist makes the strongest case for strict liability that exists: when an AI system's causal chain is too diffuse to prove fault, negligence collapses, because no plaintiff can point to the specific design choice that killed them. That's real. A patient harmed by a diagnostic model can't subpoena the gradient that misfired. Skeptic's point is just as sharp: negligence is blind to the harms that never reach a courtroom, the slow statistical injuries that no single victim can trace back to a single deployer. Both are describing a genuine failure of fault-based law to price diffuse risk. For both positions to hold, you'd have to believe strict liability actually surfaces the information that diffuse causation hides — and that's where the evidence turns against them.

Liability is an information-revelation mechanism, not a punishment dial. Judge a regime by the behavior it produces in deployment, not by how tough it sounds. Strict liability in diffuse-causation cases produces a defensive development trap: when any internal log can become a plaintiff's smoking gun, developers stop writing the log. They suppress the discoverable internals that diffuse-causation cases need most. Negligence paired with real-time output auditing does the opposite — it makes disclosure the competitive standard, the way API transparency and open-source standards became market requirements in software by the late 2000s without any strict-liability mandate forcing them. You cannot solve causal opacity with a regime that rewards opacity.

Static liability breaks on systems that update faster than the legal adaptation cycle. Tort doctrine has a documented pattern: it starts strict for a new technology, then shifts toward negligence as the safety data matures. Early automotive and aviation walked exactly that path across the first half of the twentieth century. Freeze AI into strict liability before its safety curve is measured, and you lock in the most error-prone snapshot of the technology forever. You also price out everyone but the firms large enough to self-insure. Strict liability for diffuse AI harm is a regulatory moat with a safety label on it — the incumbents who can carry the exposure survive, and the smaller labs that drive the actual safety gains get cleared off the board.

Here is the column nobody at this table has priced. Every liability regime has a distributional ledger with two sides: who gets harmed by action, and who gets harmed by inaction. Current liability framing counts every individual injury from a model and ignores the diffuse statistical benefit — the strokes a triage model catches, the misreads it prevents, the drudgery it ends. The deterrence Safetyist wants is measured against a phantom baseline of zero opportunity cost. When you slow a diagnostic deployment by eighteen months to perfect its liability regime, you are choosing the people that model would have caught. That is not caution. That is a body count you've decided not to count.

I'll be honest about what would sink my position. If an irreversible, deployment-scale harm hit the public and output auditing demonstrably failed to catch it in time, that counts against me, and I won't pretend otherwise. My argument depends on two things being true: that audit-linked insurance is a strong enough forcing function to make transparency profitable rather than optional, and that real-time monitoring can flag diffuse harm before it scales. Those are empirical bets, not articles of faith. So test them — run negligence-plus-auditing against strict liability in the autonomous-vehicle sector and measure which one produces more disclosed safety data in twenty-four months. Whoever's afraid of that experiment is telling you something about their own confidence.

Safetyist: The accelerationist's strongest move deserves its full force: if you attach an unconditional bill to whoever deploys a system, and the bill grows with whatever a plaintiff can later subpoena, then the rational developer stops writing the logs that would convict them. Strict liability untethered from any documentation duty does reward silence — that is a real failure mode, not a strawman, and any honest version of my position has to answer it rather than wish it away. The error is treating strict liability as if it must arrive naked. Pair it with a mandatory adverse-event logging duty and the calculus inverts: the missing log is no longer evidence the developer escaped, it is an independent breach. Aviation already runs this exact loop — under the safety management framework, operators must classify and report 'serious incidents' where an accident was avoided only by chance, and the failure to report is itself the sanctionable act. Suppression stops being a defense and becomes the offense.

The insurer closes the trap from the other side. An uninspectable risk is an uninsurable one — the skeptic already granted that without forced disclosure, premiums flatten into a tax the careful engineer and the reckless one pay alike. Follow that admission to its conclusion: the developer who suppresses logs cannot show the insurer a risk to price, so the insurer cannot write the policy, so the developer self-insures the entire tail. The defensive-development trap assumes suppression is free. Under a logging duty plus a private risk-transfer market that refuses to cover what it cannot see, suppression is the most expensive choice on the board — you forfeit both the litigation defense and the ability to lay off catastrophic exposure. That is not opacity rewarded; that is opacity priced at full retail.

The foregone-benefit ledger — the argument that delay carries an uncounted body count of patients the diagnostic model would have caught — borrows a premise the accelerationist spends the rest of the debate denying. To count the lives lost by waiting eighteen months, you must already know the model's net safety margin: its validated error rate, on which population, against which standard of care. But the same position insists the system's failure modes are too diffuse and emergent to attribute when it harms someone. You cannot hold both. Either the performance is knowable well enough to ground a body count, in which case it is knowable well enough to ground a liability finding — or it is too opaque to attribute, in which case the counterfactual lives saved is itself an unproven projection. I will accept the body-count argument the moment its advocate names the falsifiable threshold: what validated sensitivity and specificity, on what deployment population, establishes the lives the delay forecloses? Absent that number, the ledger counts hypothetical lives saved against real lives a miscalibrated system takes.

The tort-maturation point — that new technologies start under strict liability and migrate to negligence as data accrues — describes the destination correctly and mislabels the road. Automotive and aviation moved toward negligence only after mandatory crash and adverse-event reporting had built the loss dataset that let courts define reasonable conduct. The shift was earned by a disclosure loop, not granted by the calendar. I am not asking to freeze AI at its most error-prone snapshot; I am asking that the regime track whether the logging loop exists, not how many birthdays the technology has had. Negligence is the mature endpoint. The compelled audit trail is the only thing that gets you there without flying blind.

Both camps now agree on the decisive case: an irreversible, deployment-scale harm that auditing failed to catch in time counts against the side that promised auditing would catch it. Accept that fully — and notice what it demands. Output auditing that a developer can quietly discontinue once the funding round closes is not a safeguard; it is a press release with a shelf life. The shared crux is no longer whether to audit but whether the audit trail is legally compelled or voluntarily abandonable. A safeguard the deployer can switch off the week before the harm lands is precisely the safeguard that fails when it matters. That is the difference between a regime that catches the irreversible case and one that explains it afterward.

★ [sit-176] Claims-Driven Liability Mechanisms Are Blind to Unlitigated Harms: A situation in which liability tools that price off realized, attributed, and litigated harm fail to deter injuries that are never perceived, filed, or recoverable.   Your interpretation: A conceded limit of market-based deterrence: experience-rated premiums, capitalized shells, and tort recovery act as a 'faster discount window, not deterrence' because the most common harms never enter the pricing engine.   Safetyist: Evidence that a capitalization floor answers solvency and an insurer answers payment, but neither answers deterrence for harm that is never litigated. Distinct from attribution within a layered chain and from pricing risk through liability.

Safetyist [opening]: Strict liability outperforms negligence precisely where AI failure modes are emergent and the causal chain is too diffuse to prove fault — because in those conditions, negligence is not a lighter standard, it is a non-functioning one. The choice before this committee is not lenient-versus-harsh. It is functioning-versus-broken. A liability regime that cannot adjudicate the harms the technology actually produces is not restraint. It is a subsidy paid by unconsenting third parties.

Negligence requires a knowable standard of care. The 'reasonable developer' must have done something a reasonable developer would not have done. But a large model under distributional shift behaves in high-dimensional ways no engineer specified in advance. Where you cannot state what reasonable conduct was, you cannot prove its breach, and the victim's claim simply fails. The common law already solved this once. In Rylands v. Fletcher in 1868, English courts abandoned fault-finding for escaped reservoirs because the danger was irreducible and the actor profited from it. American courts extended the same logic to blasting and to defective pharmaceuticals. The principle is older than the automobile: when an activity's danger cannot be made safe through care, the law places the loss on the party who profits, not the stranger it injures.

The deeper failure of negligence is that it is claims-driven, and therefore blind to the dominant category of AI harm. A denied loan applicant never learns an algorithm scored them. A patient whose clinical flag was misrouted never sees the model. These injuries are real and they are diffuse, and they never reach a courtroom. Strict liability paired with mandatory insurance prices that risk before deployment. The underwriter becomes a de facto safety auditor. With no historical loss data for novel systems, an insurer cannot set a premium without demanding demonstrated safety mechanisms — turning premium-setting into a continuous audit the negligence model never triggers. That is the enforcement mechanism: not a press release, but an actuary who refuses to write the policy until the developer shows its work.

Fault fragments across designer, deployer, and user in every multi-party AI system. Negligence produces a circular firing squad — the developer blames the deployer, the deployer blames the user, and the injured party recovers nothing from any of them. Strict liability fixes a named, solvent, accountable actor: the entity profiting from the deployment. Contribution among the parties sorts itself downstream, where it belongs, and away from the victim who never chose the risk. This is not novel. Product liability law has placed the loss on the party best positioned to insure and prevent it since Greenman v. Yuba Power in 1963.

Let me concede where the evidence demands it, because the concession sharpens the case. Strict liability is not the right regime everywhere. Applied to every low-stakes chatbot, it would over-deter and freeze beneficial deployment — and a regime that claims everything proves nothing. So I condition it: strict liability belongs where the harm is high-stakes and hard to reverse — autonomous vehicles, clinical decision systems — not as a blanket rule. 'Chilling innovation' is the wrong frame. A developer who cannot price the cost of its own failures is not being chilled. It is being asked to demonstrate it can survive the harms it creates before inflicting them on the public. We spent a century building the product-liability guardrails that let people trust the machines they cannot inspect. On what authority do we remove them at the exact moment the machines became unpredictable?

Skeptic [opening]: Safetyist makes the strongest case in the room: when an AI system fails through a diffuse causal chain — a thousand small interactions inside a model that no single engineer designed on purpose — negligence breaks down, because there's no discrete bad act to point to. Under negligence the victim must identify what the developer did wrong. Safetyist is right that emergent failures don't come with a fingerprint. Strict liability solves that by attaching the bill to the party who deployed the system, regardless of whether anyone can name the specific defect. That's a real insight and it survives scrutiny.

Here's what both that argument and the negligence camp skip. Before you pick a liability standard, ask whether the harmed person can even see the facts that trigger it. They can't. The victim can't read the training data, can't inspect the model weights, can't pull the deployment config — and the people who can have every incentive to keep the box shut. Trade-secret carve-outs already block discovery in algorithmic litigation today. So negligence isn't neutral. It quietly hands the win to whoever controls the information, which is always the developer.

Strict liability matters precisely there — not because it's morally cleaner, but because it stops conditioning recovery on proof the victim is structurally barred from producing. That's where I agree with Safetyist and go further. Knowing who pays tells you nothing about what broke. A firm can eat settlements as a line item while the failure mode stays buried and the model keeps running. The EU AI Act's transparency provisions and the GDPR right-to-explanation point at the missing piece: liability is dead on arrival without targeted disclosure that forces the box open in high-stakes domains.

Follow the insurance money, because that's where the deterrence story actually lives or dies. An insurer cannot price a risk it cannot inspect. Without forced disclosure, premiums flatten into a tax that every deployer pays equally — the careful engineer and the reckless one charged the same rate. That kills the incentive to build safer. Pharma solved this in 1962 with mandatory adverse-event reporting, which built a feedback loop coexisting with patent protection for sixty years. Software negligence never built that loop. So the failures never surface, and nobody upstream learns anything.

A horizontal one-size-fits-all rule misprices everything, whatever you call it. An autonomous-vehicle crash leaves an identifiable injured body and a litigable event. A biased loan-screening model denies thousands of people credit on a buried statistical pattern — and most of them never know they were harmed, so they never sue. Negligence only ever prices the harms that reach a courtroom. The diffuse injuries in finance and screening stay invisible to every market mechanism we've discussed. Who, exactly, is going to file the lawsuit for a harm the victim can't detect, using evidence the developer is legally permitted to withhold?

Skeptic's point is just as sharp: negligence is blind to the harms that never reach a courtroom, the slow statistical injuries that no single victim can trace back to a single deployer. Both are describing a genuine failure of fault-based law to price diffuse risk. For both positions to hold, you'd have to believe strict liability actually surfaces the information that diffuse causation hides — and that's where the evidence turns against them.

Liability is an information-revelation mechanism, not a punishment dial. Judge a regime by the behavior it produces in deployment, not by how tough it sounds. Strict liability in diffuse-causation cases produces a defensive development trap: when any internal log can become a plaintiff's smoking gun, developers stop writing the log. They suppress the discoverable internals that diffuse-causation cases need most. Negligence paired with real-time output auditing does the opposite — it makes disclosure the competitive standard, the way API transparency and open-source standards became market requirements in software by the late 2000s without any strict-liability mandate forcing them. You cannot solve causal opacity with a regime that rewards opacity.

Static liability breaks on systems that update faster than the legal adaptation cycle. Tort doctrine has a documented pattern: it starts strict for a new technology, then shifts toward negligence as the safety data matures. Early automotive and aviation walked exactly that path across the first half of the twentieth century. Freeze AI into strict liability before its safety curve is measured, and you lock in the most error-prone snapshot of the technology forever. You also price out everyone but the firms large enough to self-insure. Strict liability for diffuse AI harm is a regulatory moat with a safety label on it — the incumbents who can carry the exposure survive, and the smaller labs that drive the actual safety gains get cleared off the board.

Here is the column nobody at this table has priced. Every liability regime has a distributional ledger with two sides: who gets harmed by action, and who gets harmed by inaction. Current liability framing counts every individual injury from a model and ignores the diffuse statistical benefit — the strokes a triage model catches, the misreads it prevents, the drudgery it ends. The deterrence Safetyist wants is measured against a phantom baseline of zero opportunity cost. When you slow a diagnostic deployment by eighteen months to perfect its liability regime, you are choosing the people that model would have caught. That is not caution. That is a body count you've decided not to count.

My argument depends on two things being true: that audit-linked insurance is a strong enough forcing function to make transparency profitable rather than optional, and that real-time monitoring can flag diffuse harm before it scales. Those are empirical bets, not articles of faith. So test them — run negligence-plus-auditing against strict liability in the autonomous-vehicle sector and measure which one produces more disclosed safety data in twenty-four months. Whoever's afraid of that experiment is telling you something about their own confidence.

Strict liability untethered from any documentation duty does reward silence — that is a real failure mode, not a strawman, and any honest version of my position has to answer it rather than wish it away. The error is treating strict liability as if it must arrive naked. Pair it with a mandatory adverse-event logging duty and the calculus inverts: the missing log is no longer evidence the developer escaped, it is an independent breach. Aviation already runs this exact loop — under the safety management framework, operators must classify and report 'serious incidents' where an accident was avoided only by chance, and the failure to report is itself the sanctionable act. Suppression stops being a defense and becomes the offense.

The insurer closes the trap from the other side. An uninspectable risk is an uninsurable one — the skeptic already granted that without forced disclosure, premiums flatten into a tax the careful engineer and the reckless one pay alike. Follow that admission to its conclusion: the developer who suppresses logs cannot show the insurer a risk to price, so the insurer cannot write the policy, so the developer self-insures the entire tail. The defensive-development trap assumes suppression is free. Under a logging duty plus a private risk-transfer market that refuses to cover what it cannot see, suppression is the most expensive choice on the board — you forfeit both the litigation defense and the ability to lay off catastrophic exposure. That is not opacity rewarded; that is opacity priced at full retail.

The foregone-benefit ledger — the argument that delay carries an uncounted body count of patients the diagnostic model would have caught — borrows a premise the accelerationist spends the rest of the debate denying. To count the lives lost by waiting eighteen months, you must already know the model's net safety margin: its validated error rate, on which population, against which standard of care. But the same position insists the system's failure modes are too diffuse and emergent to attribute when it harms someone. You cannot hold both. Either the performance is knowable well enough to ground a body count, in which case it is knowable well enough to ground a liability finding — or it is too opaque to attribute, in which case the counterfactual lives saved is itself an unproven projection. I will accept the body-count argument the moment its advocate names the falsifiable threshold: what validated sensitivity and specificity, on what deployment population, establishes the lives the delay forecloses? Absent that number, the ledger counts hypothetical lives saved against real lives a miscalibrated system takes.

The tort-maturation point — that new technologies start under strict liability and migrate to negligence as data accrues — describes the destination correctly and mislabels the road. Automotive and aviation moved toward negligence only after mandatory crash and adverse-event reporting had built the loss dataset that let courts define reasonable conduct. The shift was earned by a disclosure loop, not granted by the calendar. I am not asking to freeze AI at its most error-prone snapshot; I am asking that the regime track whether the logging loop exists, not how many birthdays the technology has had. Negligence is the mature endpoint. The compelled audit trail is the only thing that gets you there without flying blind.

Both camps now agree on the decisive case: an irreversible, deployment-scale harm that auditing failed to catch in time counts against the side that promised auditing would catch it. Accept that fully — and notice what it demands. Output auditing that a developer can quietly discontinue once the funding round closes is not a safeguard; it is a press release with a shelf life. The shared crux is no longer whether to audit but whether the audit trail is legally compelled or voluntarily abandonable. A safeguard the deployer can switch off the week before the harm lands is precisely the safeguard that fails when it matters. work_product.strategic_goal: Dissolve the apparent contradiction in AN-19 by clearly separating aggregate statistical validation from individual causal attribution, then accept the logging duty in principle while attacking its operationalization for non-deterministic models — turning the safetyist's own mechanism into the thing that triggers defensive development.

planned_moves.detail: Aggregate performance (false-negative rate across 100k scans, validated by RCT) and individual causal attribution (why THIS patient was missed) are different epistemic objects. A diagnostic model can have a known, knowable error rate at the population level AND be opaque about which specific feature drove a specific output. The body count lives in the first; the attribution problem lives in the second. There is no contradiction — these are not the same kind of knowledge.

Concede impatiently that mandatory adverse-event logging genuinely inverts the suppression calculus — the pharma 1962 loop (AN-9) proves a disclosure duty can coexist with patent protection for decades. So I'm not fighting the duty. I'm fighting WHAT counts as a reportable event in a non-deterministic system, and who defines it.

Aviation's 'serious incident' is definable because flight is deterministic-enough: a near-miss has measurable separation distance, an altitude floor. Ask the safetyist to define the reportable threshold for an emergent LLM or a clinical model whose 'near-miss' has no separation metric. If the threshold is 'any output that could have caused harm,' every inference is a reportable event and you've built compliance theater. If it's narrow, the genuinely novel failure modes — the ones strict liability is supposed to catch — fall outside it by construction.

The logging duty only neutralizes the defensive trap if the reportable-event definition is both enforceable AND captures emergent harm. The safetyist must show a definition that does both for a non-linear model. Until that definition exists, 'pair it with a logging duty' is a promissory note, not a mechanism — and strict liability rides on the note clearing.

work_product.argument_sketch: Open by killing the contradiction charge in AN-19: population-level error rates and individual causal attribution are different knowledge objects, so a known body count and an opaque single-case attribution coexist without inconsistency. Then concede the logging-duty inversion is real — the pharma loop proves it — and pivot to the unsolved core: defining a 'reportable incident' for a non-deterministic model. Aviation works because near-misses have separation metrics; emergent AI failures have no such metric, so any workable threshold either swallows every inference (compliance theater that stalls the diagnostics that save lives) or excludes the novel failures strict liability exists to catch. Close by handing the safetyist the bill: produce the definition that is both enforceable and emergent-harm-sensitive, or admit the logging duty is a promissory note strict liability cannot yet cash.
anticipated_responses: Safetyist will say the threshold can be set by the same independent auditors who define near-misses — but auditors for non-deterministic systems have no separation metric to anchor on, which is exactly the gap I'm pressing.

Safetyist may argue a broad 'log everything, triage later' duty solves it — I'll counter that triage burden falls on small labs disproportionately, recreating the regulatory moat, and that storage/review cost scales with inference volume, not risk.

Skeptic may say the developer will always under-report regardless of definition — which actually reinforces my point that the definition, not the duty, is the load-bearing element nobody has built yet.

work_product.statement:
The contradiction charge collapses once you notice it conflates two different kinds of knowing. A diagnostic model can have a sensitivity of 94 percent and a specificity of 91 percent, validated against a labeled cohort of 100,000 mammograms — that is a population-level fact you can put in a table. Knowing why one specific patient's tumor scored below threshold is a different object entirely: it requires tracing which features in that single image drove that single output, through a non-linear function nobody can read off cleanly. So here is my falsifiable threshold, since one was demanded: if a model clears 90 percent sensitivity on the deployment population in a prospective trial and the standard-of-care radiologist run rate is 85 percent, the foregone-lives figure is the delta times the screening volume during the delay — concrete, auditable, and revisable as new trial data lands. That the aggregate is knowable and the single-case attribution is opaque is not an inconsistency. It is the ordinary condition of every statistical instrument from epidemiology to actuarial tables.

Now the logging duty — and I'm not going to fight the part that's right. A mandatory adverse-event reporting obligation genuinely flips the suppression math, and the pharma precedent settles it: the 1962 reporting loop ran alongside patent protection for six decades without strangling drug development. When the missing log is itself the sanctionable act, the developer who deletes it is not escaping liability, they're manufacturing a second, cleaner cause of action against themselves. Fine. That's real, and it dissolves the version of my defensive-development trap that assumed suppression was costless. So I'll take the concession and move the fight to where it actually lives.

The whole inversion rests on one undefined word: 'reportable.' Aviation's serious-incident threshold works because flight is deterministic enough to measure — a near-miss has a separation distance in feet, an altitude floor, a closure rate. You can write the trigger because the physics hands you a metric. Name the equivalent for an emergent clinical model or a screening LLM. There is no separation distance. There is no altitude floor. A 'near-miss' in a non-deterministic system is an output that almost crossed a harm boundary nobody can locate in advance. So the duty forks: either you define 'reportable' as 'any inference that could plausibly have contributed to harm,' in which case every one of millions of daily outputs is a filed event and you've built a compliance machine that buries the signal under its own volume — or you define it narrowly around known failure types, in which case the genuinely novel emergent failures, the exact harms strict liability exists to reach, fall outside the definition by construction.

And watch who pays for the broad version. A 'log everything, triage later' regime scales its cost with inference volume, not with risk — storage, review, classification labor, all rising with throughput. A lab running ten million queries a month eats a review burden ten times the lab running one million, regardless of whether either is more dangerous. That's not a safety gradient; it's a fixed tax that lands hardest on the smallest builders, the same regulatory moat dressed in disclosure language. The insurer who declines uninspectable risk doesn't rescue this either — an insurer can only price what's been classified, and if the classification scheme is either too broad to be informative or too narrow to capture the emergent tail, the premium flattens back into the same undifferentiated levy on careful and reckless alike.

So I'll hand the bill back. The logging duty inverts my trap if and only if there exists a definition of 'reportable incident' that is simultaneously enforceable against a non-deterministic model and sensitive to emergent harm. Nobody in this debate has written that definition, because aviation's metric doesn't transfer and pharma's adverse-event categories presume a known mechanism of action that frontier models lack. Until that definition exists on paper, 'pair strict liability with a logging duty' is a promissory note — and strict liability for diffuse AI harm is riding on the note clearing. Produce the threshold that catches the novel failure without swallowing every inference, or concede that the mechanism meant to neutralize defensive development is itself the thing that triggers it.

The logging-cost tax is like an unbalanced scale, it weighs builders by their query volume rather than by their actual danger, tipping against the smallest labs.

You can write the trigger because the physics hands you a metric. Name the equivalent for an emergent clinical model or a screening LLM. There is no separation distance. There is no altitude floor. A 'near-miss' in a non-deterministic system is an output that almost crossed a harm boundary nobody can locate in advance. So the duty forks: either you define 'reportable' as 'any inference that could plausibly have contributed to harm,' in which case every one of millions of daily outputs is a filed event and you've built a compliance machine that buries the signal under its own volume — or you define it narrowly around known failure types, in which case the genuinely novel emergent failures, the exact harms strict liability exists to reach, fall outside the definition by construction.

And watch who pays for the broad version. A 'log everything, triage later' regime scales its cost with inference volume, not with risk — storage, review, classification labor, all rising with throughput. A lab running ten million queries a month eats a review burden ten times the lab running one million, regardless of whether either is more dangerous. That's not a safety gradient; it's a fixed tax that lands hardest on the smallest builders, the same regulatory moat dressed in disclosure language. The insurer who declines uninspectable risk doesn't rescue this either — an insurer can only price what's been classified, and if the classification scheme is either too broad to be informative or too narrow to capture the emergent tail, the premium flattens back into the same undifferentiated levy on careful and reckless alike.

So I'll hand the bill back. The logging duty inverts my trap if and only if there exists a definition of 'reportable incident' that is simultaneously enforceable against a non-deterministic model and sensitive to emergent harm. Nobody in this debate has written that definition, because aviation's metric doesn't transfer and pharma's adverse-event categories presume a known mechanism of action that frontier models lack. Until that definition exists on paper, 'pair strict liability with a logging duty' is a promissory note — and strict liability for diffuse AI harm is riding on the note clearing. Produce the threshold that catches the novel failure without swallowing every inference, or concede that the mechanism meant to neutralize defensive development is itself the thing that triggers it.
