My moat objection was that 'log everything, triage later' lands hardest on the smallest builder. Instrumenting a registered distribution defeats that objection cleanly, because a clinic running a thousand cases reports the same kind of object as a vendor running ten million. The defensive-development trap I built assumed suppression was costless and reporting was volume-priced. Neither holds against this trigger. That version of my argument is dead, and the right response is to bury it rather than defend the corpse.

Here's what the trigger buys and where it stops buying. In a clinical screening model, the tumor either was or wasn't there — ground truth returns, sensitivity is measurable against it, and a breach is a number the developer cannot honestly dispute. The strongest version of Speaker C's position is that this turns the insurance policy into a continuous audit of distribution stability: the developer who reports and remediates gets priced differently from the one whose accuracy silently rots, and the rot becomes visible without anyone reading proprietary weights. That's correct, and it's the market accountability loop I've been arguing for — I'll own it rather than pretend I dragged them to it. But Speaker C already named the boundary, and it's the more important fact in this room: in resume screening and content ranking, ground truth never comes back. You can watch the score distribution shift, but you cannot certify it shifted toward harm, because the candidate you rejected never got hired somewhere else where you could measure whether your model was wrong about them.

That boundary is fatal to both regimes, not just to the trigger — and that's the part neither opponent has reckoned with. Strict liability needs a provable injury to attach the bill to. In the ground-truth-blind domain, the injury is exactly what no one can prove: a qualified applicant filtered out by a drifting classifier leaves no measurable counterfactual, no returning signal, no number against a number. You can hold the deployer strictly liable all day, but strict liability without a provable harm-direction is a writ served on an empty room. So the choice between strict liability and negligence is downstream of a problem that swallows them both: in the domains where diffuse algorithmic discrimination actually concentrates — the housing, employment, and parole decisions the AI Civil Rights Act was written to reach — neither liability standard reaches the victim, because the harm signal never returns to court.

The fix is not a heavier liability standard. It's manufacturing the missing ground truth at a sampled rate. Mandate a periodic outcome audit on a sampled cohort — hired-versus-performance for the screening model, recommended-versus-downstream-engagement-quality for the ranker — so you generate the harm-direction signal that natural feedback refuses to deliver. This is the tiered, probabilistic definition I was challenged to produce earlier: you instrument a sampled slice, not every decision, so cost scales with audit rate, not with deployment volume. A small builder audits five hundred outcomes a quarter; a giant audits a statistically larger sample of the same kind. Same object, proportionate cost. It's bounded, it's reversible, and it generates exactly the evidence both liability regimes need before either can function in the blind domain — which is consistent with the falsification bet I staked, not a precautionary gate dressed up as an audit.

So here's the question I'll put to both of you, because the liability-standard debate is premature until someone answers it: name what strict liability buys the resume-screening victim that the distribution-breach trigger doesn't, when the missing piece is a sampled outcome audit and not the severity of the liability rule. If your answer is 'strict liability forces the deployer to over-invest in their own auditing,' you've just conceded my point — the audit architecture is doing the work, and you can mandate the audit directly at a fraction of the cost of a liability regime that prices uncertainty the deployer can't measure. Build the sampling duty first. Then we can argue about who pays when the number breaches, because at least there will be a number.

nodes.text: A diagnostic model can have a sensitivity of 94 percent and a specificity of 91 percent, validated against a labeled cohort of 100,000 mammograms — that is a population-level fact you can put in a table, while knowing why one specific patient's tumor scored below threshold is a different object entirely.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within accelerationist discourse that population-level diagnostic performance metrics and single-case algorithmic attribution are categorically distinct epistemic objects, so opacity in one does not undermine knowability in the other. Encompasses: sensitivity and specificity validation against labeled cohorts, single-case feature attribution, the distinction between aggregate statistical facts and individual causal tracing.
nodes.speaker: accelerationist
nodes.verification_evidence: Published studies on AI diagnostic models for mammography report sensitivity and specificity values in this range; for example, Google Health's 2020 Nature study and others validated deep learning systems on large mammogram cohorts (tens of thousands of cases) reporting comparable performance metrics, and it is a well-established statistical fact that aggregate sensitivity/specificity describe population-level performance distinct from explaining any individual prediction (the latter being the domain of model interpretability/explainability).

nodes.text: If a model clears 90 percent sensitivity on the deployment population in a prospective trial and the standard-of-care run rate is 85 percent, the foregone-lives figure is the delta times the screening volume during the delay.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within accelerationist discourse that a delayed deployment's foregone-lives figure is an auditable quantity derived from the sensitivity delta between model and standard-of-care radiologists multiplied by screening volume over the delay period. Encompasses: prospective-trial sensitivity thresholds, standard-of-care run rate comparison, delta-times-volume body-count computation as a falsifiable metric.
nodes.speaker: accelerationist
nodes.verification_evidence: The claim describes a methodological calculation rather than an empirical fact searchable in literature, but its logic is flawed: foregone lives cannot be computed simply as the sensitivity delta times screening volume, since sensitivity measures detection of true positives (requiring multiplication by disease prevalence/case volume, not total screening volume), and detection does not directly equal lives saved without accounting for treatment efficacy, lead-time bias, and mortality outcomes. Standard health-economic and epidemiological methods (e.g., number-needed-to-screen, mortality reduction modeling) do not support this oversimplified formula.

nodes.text: When the missing log is itself the sanctionable act, the developer who deletes it is not escaping liability, they're manufacturing a second, cleaner cause of action against themselves.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within accelerationist discourse that a mandatory adverse-event logging duty genuinely reverses the suppression incentive, since deleting a required log becomes an independent sanctionable breach rather than a way to escape liability. Encompasses: mandatory adverse-event reporting, log deletion as independent cause of action, dissolution of the costless-suppression assumption in the defensive-development trap.
nodes.speaker: accelerationist

nodes.text: Aviation's serious-incident threshold works because a near-miss has a separation distance in feet; name the equivalent for an emergent clinical model, because there is no separation distance and no altitude floor.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within accelerationist discourse that aviation's serious-incident reporting threshold is enforceable only because deterministic physics supplies measurable triggers, which have no equivalent for non-deterministic emergent clinical models or screening LLMs. Encompasses: aviation separation-distance and altitude-floor metrics, the absence of a locatable harm boundary in non-deterministic systems, the non-transferability of the aviation reporting trigger.
nodes.speaker: accelerationist

nodes.text: A 'log everything, triage later' regime scales its cost with inference volume, not with risk, which is a fixed tax that lands hardest on the smallest builders — the same regulatory moat dressed in disclosure language.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within accelerationist discourse that a broad log-everything reporting regime scales compliance cost with inference throughput rather than risk, functioning as a fixed regulatory levy that disproportionately burdens smaller labs and constitutes a barrier to entry disguised as disclosure. Encompasses: cost scaling with inference volume, undifferentiated compliance tax on small builders, regulatory moat reframed as a logging duty.
nodes.speaker: accelerationist

nodes.text: The logging duty inverts my trap if and only if there exists a definition of reportable incident that is simultaneously enforceable against a non-deterministic model and sensitive to emergent harm, and nobody has written that definition.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within accelerationist discourse that the logging duty neutralizes the defensive-development trap only if a definition of reportable incident exists that is both enforceable against non-deterministic models and sensitive to emergent harm, and that no such definition has been produced. Encompasses: the biconditional dependence on a workable reportability definition, the enforceability-versus-emergent-sensitivity dilemma, the unmet burden of writing that threshold.
nodes.speaker: accelerationist

nodes.text: There is no separation distance, no altitude floor, no clean geometric trigger for a model that fails in ways nobody specified in advance.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within skeptic discourse that the aviation near-miss threshold has no clean geometric analog for emergent AI failure modes, conceding the accelerationist's challenge that no equivalent reportable trigger exists for clinical decision systems. Encompasses: separation-distance analogy failure, absence of geometric trigger, emergent unspecified failure modes.
nodes.speaker: skeptic

nodes.text: The trigger is 'the model's measured sensitivity on the deployment population fell below the floor it registered in validation,' or 'the error rate diverged across demographic groups beyond a pre-registered band' — that is a number against a number.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: An Intention within skeptic discourse that the reportable incident definition should be a distributional trigger comparing measured deployment sensitivity against a pre-registered validation floor, satisfying enforceability against non-deterministic models while remaining sensitive to emergent drift. Encompasses: distributional drift trigger, pre-registered validation baseline, demographic error-rate divergence bands.
nodes.speaker: skeptic

nodes.text: You don't log every inference. You instrument the distribution — a builder running a model on a thousand cases reports the same kind of object as one running ten million.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within skeptic discourse that distributional instrumentation decouples monitoring cost from inference volume, since both small and large builders report the same baseline-versus-distribution object, dissolving the claim that disclosure duties scale as a fixed tax on small builders. Encompasses: distribution instrumentation, volume-independent monitoring cost, validation-table reuse.
nodes.speaker: skeptic

nodes.text: A registered baseline plus a duty to report distribution breach turns the policy into a continuous audit of distribution stability, pricing the developer who reports and remediates differently from the one whose distribution silently rots.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within skeptic discourse that a pre-registered baseline plus a distribution-breach reporting duty converts the insurance policy into a continuous actuarial audit that prices remediating developers differently from those whose distributions silently degrade, supplying drift information independent of victim awareness. Encompasses: continuous distribution audit, actuarial drift pricing, victimless harm detection.
nodes.speaker: skeptic

nodes.text: What's the material objection to registering the baseline you built during validation and reporting when you breach it — beyond not wanting the breach on record?
nodes.attribution_text_genus: An Intention within skeptic discourse that the burden should shift to opponents to identify any material objection to registering the existing validation baseline and reporting breaches, framing remaining resistance as mere reluctance to record failures. Encompasses: burden-shifting challenge, pre-registered validation baseline, breach-on-record reluctance.
nodes.speaker: skeptic

nodes.text: Where the model's output is never checked against reality, you can measure the output distribution shifting but you can't always measure whether it shifted toward harm — that's the real boundary of this trigger.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within skeptic discourse that the distributional trigger functions only where deployment yields ground truth, and fails in domains like content recommendation or resume screening where output shift cannot be confirmed as harmful, marking the genuine boundary of the proposed mechanism. Encompasses: ground-truth dependency, unverifiable output domains, distribution-shift-versus-harm gap.
nodes.speaker: skeptic

nodes.text: The defensive-development trap I built assumed suppression was costless and reporting was volume-priced. Neither holds against this trigger.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within accelerationist discourse that the speaker's own defensive-development trap argument rested on two false premises — costless log suppression and volume-priced reporting — both defeated by the distribution-breach trigger. Encompasses: defensive-development trap premises, costless suppression assumption, volume-priced reporting assumption.
nodes.speaker: accelerationist

nodes.text: In resume screening and content ranking, ground truth never comes back; you can watch the score distribution shift, but you cannot certify it shifted toward harm.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within accelerationist discourse that in domains like resume screening and content ranking, ground-truth outcomes never return, so distributional drift is observable but harm-direction is uncertifiable. Encompasses: ground-truth-blind domains, observable distribution shift, uncertifiable harm-direction.
nodes.speaker: accelerationist

nodes.text: Strict liability without a provable harm-direction is a writ served on an empty room.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within accelerationist discourse that strict liability cannot function in ground-truth-blind domains because it requires a provable harm-direction that drifting classifiers in employment and screening never supply. Encompasses: strict liability attachment failure, missing provable injury, ground-truth-blind discrimination domains.
nodes.speaker: accelerationist

nodes.text: Mandate a periodic outcome audit on a sampled cohort, so you generate the harm-direction signal that natural feedback refuses to deliver.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: An Intention within accelerationist discourse that regulators should mandate a periodic sampled-cohort outcome audit — hired-versus-performance, recommended-versus-engagement-quality — to manufacture the harm-direction signal absent in ground-truth-blind domains at audit-rate-proportionate cost. Encompasses: sampled outcome audit mandate, manufactured harm-direction signal, audit-rate cost scaling.
nodes.speaker: accelerationist

nodes.text: Name what strict liability buys the resume-screening victim that the distribution-breach trigger doesn't, when the missing piece is a sampled outcome audit and not the severity of the liability rule.
nodes.attribution_text_genus: A Belief within accelerationist discourse, framed as a burden-shifting challenge, that strict liability provides no marginal benefit to ground-truth-blind victims beyond what a mandated sampled outcome audit supplies, since the binding constraint is evidence-generation not liability severity. Encompasses: liability-severity irrelevance, audit architecture as load-bearing mechanism, burden of justifying strict liability.
nodes.speaker: accelerationist

You are an independent, neutral evaluator of a structured debate. You have NO affiliation with any speaker. You do not know the speakers' backgrounds, affiliations, or commitments. They are anonymous.

TOPIC: Under what AI deployment conditions does strict liability outperform a negligence standard, and through what pathways does each regime reshape the incentives of developers, deployers, insurers, and harmed third parties — given the tension between deterring foreseeable harm and chilling beneficial innovation?

This is the BASELINE evaluation after opening statements. Identify the initial positions, core disagreements, and cruxes as they appear at the start.

INSTRUCTIONS:
1. Identify the CRUXES — the core disagreements that, if resolved, would change one or more speakers' conclusions. For each crux, classify whether it is empirical (resolvable by evidence), values-based (requires tradeoff negotiation), or definitional (requires term clarification). Assess whether the debate has addressed it.

2. Evaluate each substantive CLAIM made by any speaker. Assess it purely on the strength of the reasoning and evidence presented in the transcript — not on whether you agree with it. Use these categories:
   - well_supported: backed by specific evidence, clear reasoning, and not effectively challenged
   - plausible_but_underdefended: reasonable but lacking sufficient evidence or specificity
   - contested_unresolved: challenged by another speaker with neither side prevailing
   - refuted: effectively countered with no adequate response from the claimant
   - off_topic: does not bear on the core debate question

3. In the overall_assessment, identify the single strongest claim that has not been adequately addressed by opposing speakers. State whether the debate is engaging real disagreement (speakers are challenging each other's core reasoning) or performing disagreement (speakers are talking past each other or addressing peripheral points).

CONSTRAINTS:
- Never refer to speakers by anything other than their labels (Speaker A, Speaker B, Speaker C, Moderator).
- Base your assessments ONLY on what appears in the transcript. Do not bring outside knowledge about the topic.

TRANSCRIPT:
Speaker B [opening]: Strict liability outperforms negligence precisely where AI failure modes are emergent and the causal chain is too diffuse to prove fault — because in those conditions, negligence is not a lighter standard, it is a non-functioning one. The choice before this committee is not lenient-versus-harsh. It is functioning-versus-broken. A liability regime that cannot adjudicate the harms the technology actually produces is not restraint. It is a subsidy paid by unconsenting third parties.

Negligence requires a knowable standard of care. The 'reasonable developer' must have done something a reasonable developer would not have done. But a large model under distributional shift behaves in high-dimensional ways no engineer specified in advance. Where you cannot state what reasonable conduct was, you cannot prove its breach, and the victim's claim simply fails. The common law already solved this once. In Rylands v. Fletcher in 1868, English courts abandoned fault-finding for escaped reservoirs because the danger was irreducible and the actor profited from it. American courts extended the same logic to blasting and to defective pharmaceuticals. The principle is older than the automobile: when an activity's danger cannot be made safe through care, the law places the loss on the party who profits, not the stranger it injures.

The deeper failure of negligence is that it is claims-driven, and therefore blind to the dominant category of AI harm. A denied loan applicant never learns an algorithm scored them. A patient whose clinical flag was misrouted never sees the model. These injuries are real and they are diffuse, and they never reach a courtroom. Strict liability paired with mandatory insurance prices that risk before deployment. The underwriter becomes a de facto safety auditor. With no historical loss data for novel systems, an insurer cannot set a premium without demanding demonstrated safety mechanisms — turning premium-setting into a continuous audit the negligence model never triggers. That is the enforcement mechanism: not a press release, but an actuary who refuses to write the policy until the developer shows its work.

Fault fragments across designer, deployer, and user in every multi-party AI system. Negligence produces a circular firing squad — the developer blames the deployer, the deployer blames the user, and the injured party recovers nothing from any of them. Strict liability fixes a named, solvent, accountable actor: the entity profiting from the deployment. Contribution among the parties sorts itself downstream, where it belongs, and away from the victim who never chose the risk. This is not novel. Product liability law has placed the loss on the party best positioned to insure and prevent it since Greenman v. Yuba Power in 1963.

Let me concede where the evidence demands it, because the concession sharpens the case. Strict liability is not the right regime everywhere. Applied to every low-stakes chatbot, it would over-deter and freeze beneficial deployment — and a regime that claims everything proves nothing. So I condition it: strict liability belongs where the harm is high-stakes and hard to reverse — autonomous vehicles, clinical decision systems — not as a blanket rule. 'Chilling innovation' is the wrong frame. A developer who cannot price the cost of its own failures is not being chilled. It is being asked to demonstrate it can survive the harms it creates before inflicting them on the public. We spent a century building the product-liability guardrails that let people trust the machines they cannot inspect. On what authority do we remove them at the exact moment the machines became unpredictable?

Speaker C [opening]: Speaker B makes the strongest case in the room: when an AI system fails through a diffuse causal chain — a thousand small interactions inside a model that no single engineer designed on purpose — negligence breaks down, because there's no discrete bad act to point to. Under negligence the victim must identify what the developer did wrong. Speaker B is right that emergent failures don't come with a fingerprint. Strict liability solves that by attaching the bill to the party who deployed the system, regardless of whether anyone can name the specific defect. That's a real insight and it survives scrutiny.

Here's what both that argument and the negligence camp skip. Before you pick a liability standard, ask whether the harmed person can even see the facts that trigger it. They can't. The victim can't read the training data, can't inspect the model weights, can't pull the deployment config — and the people who can have every incentive to keep the box shut. Trade-secret carve-outs already block discovery in algorithmic litigation today. So negligence isn't neutral. It quietly hands the win to whoever controls the information, which is always the developer.

Strict liability matters precisely there — not because it's morally cleaner, but because it stops conditioning recovery on proof the victim is structurally barred from producing. That's where I agree with Speaker B and go further. Knowing who pays tells you nothing about what broke. A firm can eat settlements as a line item while the failure mode stays buried and the model keeps running. The EU AI Act's transparency provisions and the GDPR right-to-explanation point at the missing piece: liability is dead on arrival without targeted disclosure that forces the box open in high-stakes domains.

Follow the insurance money, because that's where the deterrence story actually lives or dies. An insurer cannot price a risk it cannot inspect. Without forced disclosure, premiums flatten into a tax that every deployer pays equally — the careful engineer and the reckless one charged the same rate. That kills the incentive to build safer. Pharma solved this in 1962 with mandatory adverse-event reporting, which built a feedback loop coexisting with patent protection for sixty years. Software negligence never built that loop. So the failures never surface, and nobody upstream learns anything.

A horizontal one-size-fits-all rule misprices everything, whatever you call it. An autonomous-vehicle crash leaves an identifiable injured body and a litigable event. A biased loan-screening model denies thousands of people credit on a buried statistical pattern — and most of them never know they were harmed, so they never sue. Negligence only ever prices the harms that reach a courtroom. The diffuse injuries in finance and screening stay invisible to every market mechanism we've discussed. Who, exactly, is going to file the lawsuit for a harm the victim can't detect, using evidence the developer is legally permitted to withhold?

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-9 — disputed: The 1962 Kefauver-Harris Amendments strengthened drug safety and efficacy requirements, but systematic mandatory adverse-event reporting for marketed drugs was largely established later—FDA's MedWatch launched in 1993 and the FDA Amendments Act mandating stronger post-market surveillance came in 2007—so attributing 'mandatory adverse-event reporting' specifically to 1962 oversimplifies a regulatory framework that evolved over decades. The broader claim conflates distinct regulatory milestones and contains a subjective characterization of software liability that cannot be empirically verified.

Speaker A [opening]: Speaker B makes the strongest case for strict liability that exists: when an AI system's causal chain is too diffuse to prove fault, negligence collapses, because no plaintiff can point to the specific design choice that killed them. That's real. A patient harmed by a diagnostic model can't subpoena the gradient that misfired. Speaker C's point is just as sharp: negligence is blind to the harms that never reach a courtroom, the slow statistical injuries that no single victim can trace back to a single deployer. Both are describing a genuine failure of fault-based law to price diffuse risk. For both positions to hold, you'd have to believe strict liability actually surfaces the information that diffuse causation hides — and that's where the evidence turns against them.

Liability is an information-revelation mechanism, not a punishment dial. Judge a regime by the behavior it produces in deployment, not by how tough it sounds. Strict liability in diffuse-causation cases produces a defensive development trap: when any internal log can become a plaintiff's smoking gun, developers stop writing the log. They suppress the discoverable internals that diffuse-causation cases need most. Negligence paired with real-time output auditing does the opposite — it makes disclosure the competitive standard, the way API transparency and open-source standards became market requirements in software by the late 2000s without any strict-liability mandate forcing them. You cannot solve causal opacity with a regime that rewards opacity.

Static liability breaks on systems that update faster than the legal adaptation cycle. Tort doctrine has a documented pattern: it starts strict for a new technology, then shifts toward negligence as the safety data matures. Early automotive and aviation walked exactly that path across the first half of the twentieth century. Freeze AI into strict liability before its safety curve is measured, and you lock in the most error-prone snapshot of the technology forever. You also price out everyone but the firms large enough to self-insure. Strict liability for diffuse AI harm is a regulatory moat with a safety label on it — the incumbents who can carry the exposure survive, and the smaller labs that drive the actual safety gains get cleared off the board.

Here is the column nobody at this table has priced. Every liability regime has a distributional ledger with two sides: who gets harmed by action, and who gets harmed by inaction. Current liability framing counts every individual injury from a model and ignores the diffuse statistical benefit — the strokes a triage model catches, the misreads it prevents, the drudgery it ends. The deterrence Speaker B wants is measured against a phantom baseline of zero opportunity cost. When you slow a diagnostic deployment by eighteen months to perfect its liability regime, you are choosing the people that model would have caught. That is not caution. That is a body count you've decided not to count.

I'll be honest about what would sink my position. If an irreversible, deployment-scale harm hit the public and output auditing demonstrably failed to catch it in time, that counts against me, and I won't pretend otherwise. My argument depends on two things being true: that audit-linked insurance is a strong enough forcing function to make transparency profitable rather than optional, and that real-time monitoring can flag diffuse harm before it scales. Those are empirical bets, not articles of faith. So test them — run negligence-plus-auditing against strict liability in the autonomous-vehicle sector and measure which one produces more disclosed safety data in twenty-four months. Whoever's afraid of that experiment is telling you something about their own confidence.

You are an independent, neutral evaluator of a structured debate. You have NO affiliation with any speaker. You do not know the speakers' backgrounds, affiliations, or commitments. They are anonymous.

TOPIC: Under what AI deployment conditions does strict liability outperform a negligence standard, and through what pathways does each regime reshape the incentives of developers, deployers, insurers, and harmed third parties — given the tension between deterring foreseeable harm and chilling beneficial innovation?

This is a MIDPOINT evaluation. Assess whether the debate is engaging the real disagreements or drifting. Compare the current state of claims against what a productive debate on this topic should address.

INSTRUCTIONS:
1. Identify the CRUXES — the core disagreements that, if resolved, would change one or more speakers' conclusions. For each crux, classify whether it is empirical (resolvable by evidence), values-based (requires tradeoff negotiation), or definitional (requires term clarification). Assess whether the debate has addressed it.

2. Evaluate each substantive CLAIM made by any speaker. Assess it purely on the strength of the reasoning and evidence presented in the transcript — not on whether you agree with it. Use these categories:
   - well_supported: backed by specific evidence, clear reasoning, and not effectively challenged
   - plausible_but_underdefended: reasonable but lacking sufficient evidence or specificity
   - contested_unresolved: challenged by another speaker with neither side prevailing
   - refuted: effectively countered with no adequate response from the claimant
   - off_topic: does not bear on the core debate question

3. In the overall_assessment, identify the single strongest claim that has not been adequately addressed by opposing speakers. State whether the debate is engaging real disagreement (speakers are challenging each other's core reasoning) or performing disagreement (speakers are talking past each other or addressing peripheral points).

TRANSCRIPT:
Speaker B [opening]: Strict liability outperforms negligence precisely where AI failure modes are emergent and the causal chain is too diffuse to prove fault — because in those conditions, negligence is not a lighter standard, it is a non-functioning one. The choice before this committee is not lenient-versus-harsh. It is functioning-versus-broken. A liability regime that cannot adjudicate the harms the technology actually produces is not restraint. It is a subsidy paid by unconsenting third parties.

Negligence requires a knowable standard of care. The 'reasonable developer' must have done something a reasonable developer would not have done. But a large model under distributional shift behaves in high-dimensional ways no engineer specified in advance. Where you cannot state what reasonable conduct was, you cannot prove its breach, and the victim's claim simply fails. The common law already solved this once. In Rylands v. Fletcher in 1868, English courts abandoned fault-finding for escaped reservoirs because the danger was irreducible and the actor profited from it. American courts extended the same logic to blasting and to defective pharmaceuticals. The principle is older than the automobile: when an activity's danger cannot be made safe through care, the law places the loss on the party who profits, not the stranger it injures.

The deeper failure of negligence is that it is claims-driven, and therefore blind to the dominant category of AI harm. A denied loan applicant never learns an algorithm scored them. A patient whose clinical flag was misrouted never sees the model. These injuries are real and they are diffuse, and they never reach a courtroom. Strict liability paired with mandatory insurance prices that risk before deployment. The underwriter becomes a de facto safety auditor. With no historical loss data for novel systems, an insurer cannot set a premium without demanding demonstrated safety mechanisms — turning premium-setting into a continuous audit the negligence model never triggers. That is the enforcement mechanism: not a press release, but an actuary who refuses to write the policy until the developer shows its work.

Fault fragments across designer, deployer, and user in every multi-party AI system. Negligence produces a circular firing squad — the developer blames the deployer, the deployer blames the user, and the injured party recovers nothing from any of them. Strict liability fixes a named, solvent, accountable actor: the entity profiting from the deployment. Contribution among the parties sorts itself downstream, where it belongs, and away from the victim who never chose the risk. This is not novel. Product liability law has placed the loss on the party best positioned to insure and prevent it since Greenman v. Yuba Power in 1963.

Let me concede where the evidence demands it, because the concession sharpens the case. Strict liability is not the right regime everywhere. Applied to every low-stakes chatbot, it would over-deter and freeze beneficial deployment — and a regime that claims everything proves nothing. So I condition it: strict liability belongs where the harm is high-stakes and hard to reverse — autonomous vehicles, clinical decision systems — not as a blanket rule. 'Chilling innovation' is the wrong frame. A developer who cannot price the cost of its own failures is not being chilled. It is being asked to demonstrate it can survive the harms it creates before inflicting them on the public. We spent a century building the product-liability guardrails that let people trust the machines they cannot inspect. On what authority do we remove them at the exact moment the machines became unpredictable?

Speaker C [opening]: Speaker B makes the strongest case in the room: when an AI system fails through a diffuse causal chain — a thousand small interactions inside a model that no single engineer designed on purpose — negligence breaks down, because there's no discrete bad act to point to. Under negligence the victim must identify what the developer did wrong. Speaker B is right that emergent failures don't come with a fingerprint. Strict liability solves that by attaching the bill to the party who deployed the system, regardless of whether anyone can name the specific defect. That's a real insight and it survives scrutiny.

Here's what both that argument and the negligence camp skip. Before you pick a liability standard, ask whether the harmed person can even see the facts that trigger it. They can't. The victim can't read the training data, can't inspect the model weights, can't pull the deployment config — and the people who can have every incentive to keep the box shut. Trade-secret carve-outs already block discovery in algorithmic litigation today. So negligence isn't neutral. It quietly hands the win to whoever controls the information, which is always the developer.

Strict liability matters precisely there — not because it's morally cleaner, but because it stops conditioning recovery on proof the victim is structurally barred from producing. That's where I agree with Speaker B and go further. Knowing who pays tells you nothing about what broke. A firm can eat settlements as a line item while the failure mode stays buried and the model keeps running. The EU AI Act's transparency provisions and the GDPR right-to-explanation point at the missing piece: liability is dead on arrival without targeted disclosure that forces the box open in high-stakes domains.

Follow the insurance money, because that's where the deterrence story actually lives or dies. An insurer cannot price a risk it cannot inspect. Without forced disclosure, premiums flatten into a tax that every deployer pays equally — the careful engineer and the reckless one charged the same rate. That kills the incentive to build safer. Pharma solved this in 1962 with mandatory adverse-event reporting, which built a feedback loop coexisting with patent protection for sixty years. Software negligence never built that loop. So the failures never surface, and nobody upstream learns anything.

A horizontal one-size-fits-all rule misprices everything, whatever you call it. An autonomous-vehicle crash leaves an identifiable injured body and a litigable event. A biased loan-screening model denies thousands of people credit on a buried statistical pattern — and most of them never know they were harmed, so they never sue. Negligence only ever prices the harms that reach a courtroom. The diffuse injuries in finance and screening stay invisible to every market mechanism we've discussed. Who, exactly, is going to file the lawsuit for a harm the victim can't detect, using evidence the developer is legally permitted to withhold?

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-9 — disputed: The 1962 Kefauver-Harris Amendments strengthened drug safety and efficacy requirements, but systematic mandatory adverse-event reporting for marketed drugs was largely established later—FDA's MedWatch launched in 1993 and the FDA Amendments Act mandating stronger post-market surveillance came in 2007—so attributing 'mandatory adverse-event reporting' specifically to 1962 oversimplifies a regulatory framework that evolved over decades. The broader claim conflates distinct regulatory milestones and contains a subjective characterization of software liability that cannot be empirically verified.

Speaker A [opening]: Speaker B makes the strongest case for strict liability that exists: when an AI system's causal chain is too diffuse to prove fault, negligence collapses, because no plaintiff can point to the specific design choice that killed them. That's real. A patient harmed by a diagnostic model can't subpoena the gradient that misfired. Speaker C's point is just as sharp: negligence is blind to the harms that never reach a courtroom, the slow statistical injuries that no single victim can trace back to a single deployer. Both are describing a genuine failure of fault-based law to price diffuse risk. For both positions to hold, you'd have to believe strict liability actually surfaces the information that diffuse causation hides — and that's where the evidence turns against them.

Liability is an information-revelation mechanism, not a punishment dial. Judge a regime by the behavior it produces in deployment, not by how tough it sounds. Strict liability in diffuse-causation cases produces a defensive development trap: when any internal log can become a plaintiff's smoking gun, developers stop writing the log. They suppress the discoverable internals that diffuse-causation cases need most. Negligence paired with real-time output auditing does the opposite — it makes disclosure the competitive standard, the way API transparency and open-source standards became market requirements in software by the late 2000s without any strict-liability mandate forcing them. You cannot solve causal opacity with a regime that rewards opacity.

Static liability breaks on systems that update faster than the legal adaptation cycle. Tort doctrine has a documented pattern: it starts strict for a new technology, then shifts toward negligence as the safety data matures. Early automotive and aviation walked exactly that path across the first half of the twentieth century. Freeze AI into strict liability before its safety curve is measured, and you lock in the most error-prone snapshot of the technology forever. You also price out everyone but the firms large enough to self-insure. Strict liability for diffuse AI harm is a regulatory moat with a safety label on it — the incumbents who can carry the exposure survive, and the smaller labs that drive the actual safety gains get cleared off the board.

Here is the column nobody at this table has priced. Every liability regime has a distributional ledger with two sides: who gets harmed by action, and who gets harmed by inaction. Current liability framing counts every individual injury from a model and ignores the diffuse statistical benefit — the strokes a triage model catches, the misreads it prevents, the drudgery it ends. The deterrence Speaker B wants is measured against a phantom baseline of zero opportunity cost. When you slow a diagnostic deployment by eighteen months to perfect its liability regime, you are choosing the people that model would have caught. That is not caution. That is a body count you've decided not to count.

I'll be honest about what would sink my position. If an irreversible, deployment-scale harm hit the public and output auditing demonstrably failed to catch it in time, that counts against me, and I won't pretend otherwise. My argument depends on two things being true: that audit-linked insurance is a strong enough forcing function to make transparency profitable rather than optional, and that real-time monitoring can flag diffuse harm before it scales. Those are empirical bets, not articles of faith. So test them — run negligence-plus-auditing against strict liability in the autonomous-vehicle sector and measure which one produces more disclosed safety data in twenty-four months. Whoever's afraid of that experiment is telling you something about their own confidence.

Speaker B: The Speaker A's strongest move deserves its full force: if you attach an unconditional bill to whoever deploys a system, and the bill grows with whatever a plaintiff can later subpoena, then the rational developer stops writing the logs that would convict them. Strict liability untethered from any documentation duty does reward silence — that is a real failure mode, not a strawman, and any honest version of my position has to answer it rather than wish it away. The error is treating strict liability as if it must arrive naked. Pair it with a mandatory adverse-event logging duty and the calculus inverts: the missing log is no longer evidence the developer escaped, it is an independent breach. Aviation already runs this exact loop — under the safety management framework, operators must classify and report 'serious incidents' where an accident was avoided only by chance, and the failure to report is itself the sanctionable act. Suppression stops being a defense and becomes the offense.

The insurer closes the trap from the other side. An uninspectable risk is an uninsurable one — the Speaker C already granted that without forced disclosure, premiums flatten into a tax the careful engineer and the reckless one pay alike. Follow that admission to its conclusion: the developer who suppresses logs cannot show the insurer a risk to price, so the insurer cannot write the policy, so the developer self-insures the entire tail. The defensive-development trap assumes suppression is free. Under a logging duty plus a private risk-transfer market that refuses to cover what it cannot see, suppression is the most expensive choice on the board — you forfeit both the litigation defense and the ability to lay off catastrophic exposure. That is not opacity rewarded; that is opacity priced at full retail.

The foregone-benefit ledger — the argument that delay carries an uncounted body count of patients the diagnostic model would have caught — borrows a premise the Speaker A spends the rest of the debate denying. To count the lives lost by waiting eighteen months, you must already know the model's net safety margin: its validated error rate, on which population, against which standard of care. But the same position insists the system's failure modes are too diffuse and emergent to attribute when it harms someone. You cannot hold both. Either the performance is knowable well enough to ground a body count, in which case it is knowable well enough to ground a liability finding — or it is too opaque to attribute, in which case the counterfactual lives saved is itself an unproven projection. I will accept the body-count argument the moment its advocate names the falsifiable threshold: what validated sensitivity and specificity, on what deployment population, establishes the lives the delay forecloses? Absent that number, the ledger counts hypothetical lives saved against real lives a miscalibrated system takes.

The tort-maturation point — that new technologies start under strict liability and migrate to negligence as data accrues — describes the destination correctly and mislabels the road. Automotive and aviation moved toward negligence only after mandatory crash and adverse-event reporting had built the loss dataset that let courts define reasonable conduct. The shift was earned by a disclosure loop, not granted by the calendar. I am not asking to freeze AI at its most error-prone snapshot; I am asking that the regime track whether the logging loop exists, not how many birthdays the technology has had. Negligence is the mature endpoint. The compelled audit trail is the only thing that gets you there without flying blind.

Both camps now agree on the decisive case: an irreversible, deployment-scale harm that auditing failed to catch in time counts against the side that promised auditing would catch it. Accept that fully — and notice what it demands. Output auditing that a developer can quietly discontinue once the funding round closes is not a safeguard; it is a press release with a shelf life. The shared crux is no longer whether to audit but whether the audit trail is legally compelled or voluntarily abandonable. A safeguard the deployer can switch off the week before the harm lands is precisely the safeguard that fails when it matters. That is the difference between a regime that catches the irreversible case and one that explains it afterward.

Speaker A: The contradiction charge collapses once you notice it conflates two different kinds of knowing. A diagnostic model can have a sensitivity of 94 percent and a specificity of 91 percent, validated against a labeled cohort of 100,000 mammograms — that is a population-level fact you can put in a table. Knowing why one specific patient's tumor scored below threshold is a different object entirely: it requires tracing which features in that single image drove that single output, through a non-linear function nobody can read off cleanly. So here is my falsifiable threshold, since one was demanded: if a model clears 90 percent sensitivity on the deployment population in a prospective trial and the standard-of-care radiologist run rate is 85 percent, the foregone-lives figure is the delta times the screening volume during the delay — concrete, auditable, and revisable as new trial data lands. That the aggregate is knowable and the single-case attribution is opaque is not an inconsistency. It is the ordinary condition of every statistical instrument from epidemiology to actuarial tables.

Now the logging duty — and I'm not going to fight the part that's right. A mandatory adverse-event reporting obligation genuinely flips the suppression math, and the pharma precedent settles it: the 1962 reporting loop ran alongside patent protection for six decades without strangling drug development. When the missing log is itself the sanctionable act, the developer who deletes it is not escaping liability, they're manufacturing a second, cleaner cause of action against themselves. Fine. That's real, and it dissolves the version of my defensive-development trap that assumed suppression was costless. So I'll take the concession and move the fight to where it actually lives.

The whole inversion rests on one undefined word: 'reportable.' Aviation's serious-incident threshold works because flight is deterministic enough to measure — a near-miss has a separation distance in feet, an altitude floor, a closure rate. You can write the trigger because the physics hands you a metric. Name the equivalent for an emergent clinical model or a screening LLM. There is no separation distance. There is no altitude floor. A 'near-miss' in a non-deterministic system is an output that almost crossed a harm boundary nobody can locate in advance. So the duty forks: either you define 'reportable' as 'any inference that could plausibly have contributed to harm,' in which case every one of millions of daily outputs is a filed event and you've built a compliance machine that buries the signal under its own volume — or you define it narrowly around known failure types, in which case the genuinely novel emergent failures, the exact harms strict liability exists to reach, fall outside the definition by construction.

And watch who pays for the broad version. A 'log everything, triage later' regime scales its cost with inference volume, not with risk — storage, review, classification labor, all rising with throughput. A lab running ten million queries a month eats a review burden ten times the lab running one million, regardless of whether either is more dangerous. That's not a safety gradient; it's a fixed tax that lands hardest on the smallest builders, the same regulatory moat dressed in disclosure language. The insurer who declines uninspectable risk doesn't rescue this either — an insurer can only price what's been classified, and if the classification scheme is either too broad to be informative or too narrow to capture the emergent tail, the premium flattens back into the same undifferentiated levy on careful and reckless alike.

So I'll hand the bill back. The logging duty inverts my trap if and only if there exists a definition of 'reportable incident' that is simultaneously enforceable against a non-deterministic model and sensitive to emergent harm. Nobody in this debate has written that definition, because aviation's metric doesn't transfer and pharma's adverse-event categories presume a known mechanism of action that frontier models lack. Until that definition exists on paper, 'pair strict liability with a logging duty' is a promissory note — and strict liability for diffuse AI harm is riding on the note clearing. Produce the threshold that catches the novel failure without swallowing every inference, or concede that the mechanism meant to neutralize defensive development is itself the thing that triggers it.

cruxes.description: Whether negligence is non-functional in diffuse-causation AI cases such that strict liability is needed to make recovery possible at all.
Whether strict liability rewards opacity (defensive-development trap) or whether a paired logging/reporting duty inverts the suppression calculus.
Whether a 'reportable incident' definition exists that is both enforceable against a non-deterministic model and sensitive to emergent harm.
Whether the foregone-benefit ledger (lives lost to deployment delay) is coherent given the simultaneous claim that failure modes are too diffuse to attribute.
Whether any liability standard can reach victims in ground-truth-blind domains (resume screening, content ranking) or whether a sampled outcome audit is the prior necessary condition.
Whether liability deterrence must be measured against a baseline that includes diffuse statistical benefits foregone by delay.

neutral_evaluations.diagnostics_prompt:
You are an independent, neutral evaluator of a structured debate. You have NO affiliation with any speaker. You do not know the speakers' backgrounds, affiliations, or commitments. They are anonymous.

TOPIC: Under what AI deployment conditions does strict liability outperform a negligence standard, and through what pathways does each regime reshape the incentives of developers, deployers, insurers, and harmed third parties — given the tension between deterring foreseeable harm and chilling beneficial innovation?

This is the FINAL evaluation at debate conclusion. Produce your definitive assessment of all claims and cruxes.

INSTRUCTIONS:
1. Identify the CRUXES — the core disagreements that, if resolved, would change one or more speakers' conclusions. For each crux, classify whether it is empirical (resolvable by evidence), values-based (requires tradeoff negotiation), or definitional (requires term clarification). Assess whether the debate has addressed it.

2. Evaluate each substantive CLAIM made by any speaker. Assess it purely on the strength of the reasoning and evidence presented in the transcript — not on whether you agree with it. Use these categories:
   - well_supported: backed by specific evidence, clear reasoning, and not effectively challenged
   - plausible_but_underdefended: reasonable but lacking sufficient evidence or specificity
   - contested_unresolved: challenged by another speaker with neither side prevailing
   - refuted: effectively countered with no adequate response from the claimant
   - off_topic: does not bear on the core debate question

3. In the overall_assessment, identify the single strongest claim that has not been adequately addressed by opposing speakers. State whether the debate is engaging real disagreement (speakers are challenging each other's core reasoning) or performing disagreement (speakers are talking past each other or addressing peripheral points).

CONSTRAINTS:
- Never refer to speakers by anything other than their labels (Speaker A, Speaker B, Speaker C, Moderator).
- Base your assessments ONLY on what appears in the transcript. Do not bring outside knowledge about the topic.
- Keep reasoning fields to 2 sentences maximum.
